paras: The Seattle lynchings of 1882 were the hangings of James Sullivan, William Howard and Benjamin Payne by a citizens' Committee of Safety on Occidental Square in Seattle, Washington Territory, on January 18, 1882. Sullivan and Howard were seized from officers as soon as a justice ended their hearing on a charge of murdering George B. Reynolds, and Payne, held for killing a police officer, was then taken from the county jail. A coroner's jury called the deaths 'speedy and substantial justice', and much of the Pacific Coast press praised the committee.

In October 1881 Seattle police officer Sires was shot, according to a Seattle dispatch, 'by a vagrant named Payne', who was then held in the county jail. On January 17, 1882, two men stopped Reynolds, a head salesman, in the street and ordered him to throw up his hands; when he reached for his revolver one of them shot him, and he died about two hours later. The fire bell was rung, business was suspended, and some 200 to 400 men organized a vigilance committee at the engine-house.

About 10 p.m. a squad of the committee found Sullivan, a one-armed man, and Howard hiding in hay on a wharf and handed them to Sheriff Wyckoff and Police Chief McGraw. Some 200 committee men then demanded the prisoners at the jail and left only after the officers promised a hearing in the morning and gave up the men's shoes for comparison with tracks.

The next morning Justice Coombs heard 28 or 29 witnesses in Yesler's Hall, with Chief Justice Greene of the territorial supreme court on the bench, while the committee hung a timber between two trees on Occidental Square. When Coombs remanded the prisoners for the grand jury, men seized every officer in the room, carried Sullivan and Howard to the square and hanged them from a wagon. Greene tried to cut the ropes with a knife but was overpowered and removed.

About 400 men, or 500 by the San Francisco Chronicle's count, then broke into the county jail with axes and sledge hammers and took Payne. Saying 'If you hang me you will hang an innocent man,' he was hanged between the other two about 1:30 p.m., and the three were buried that evening.

A coroner's jury before S. F. Coombs, acting coroner, found the men dead by hanging but was 'unable to find at whose hands'; one of its signers was an O. Jacobs, the name of the lawyer who had assisted the prosecution. The committee kept its organization and announced that highway robbers in the city would be put to death. No report of an arrest or indictment of any committee member appears in the coverage. In April a judge's address printed in the Seattle Post-Intelligencer said that those who 'killed Howard, Sullivan and Payne' could not be excused by a 'sense of duty'.

The first full account, a special telegram in the Sacramento Record-Union, ran under 'Judge Lynch' and closed with 'Everybody satisfied', calling the proceedings 'thoroughly orderly' and led by 'the business men and leading citizens of the town'. The Post-Intelligencer, as reprinted in Honolulu, insisted 'this was the work of no mob' and quoted the Portland Oregonian: 'Good men everywhere will say well done to the Committee of Safety.' The Vancouver Independent called it a 'neck-tie party' and blamed slow courts, and the Sag Harbor Express, mourning Reynolds as a native son, wished Guiteau had been 'served the same way'.

Elsewhere the story ran as a short wire under 'Murderers Lynched' or 'Lynch Law', some versions placing Seattle in 'Wyoming Territory'. Criticism came later: in February the Walla Walla Statesman urged its readers not to allow 'such a lynching as recently occurred in Seattle'. No account read gives the race of any of the three men.

Most accounts and the coroner's verdict put the shooting on the 17th and the hangings on the 18th, but the Post-Intelligencer text reprinted in Honolulu dates them to the 18th and 19th. Crowd estimates ranged from 'several hundred' in the wire to 800 or 1,000 in the Chronicle and about 2,000 in the Post-Intelligencer and the Vancouver Independent.

bases: An organized Committee of Safety seized two men from a justice's hearing and a third from the county jail and hanged all three on Occidental Square (A2, A16, A21).

Three men in official custody were hanged by a committee of hundreds that overpowered the sheriff, police and jailers (A2, A6, A21); the men were accused of murders, and the committee presented the hangings as 'speedy and substantial justice' (A21, A13).

A special telegram (A2), the AP wire (A3, A6), the territorial press (A7, A13, A15), the San Francisco Chronicle (A16) and the Seattle Post-Intelligencer as quoted in Honolulu (A20, A21) agree on the seizures, the three hangings and the coroner's verdict.

accounts.label: Seattle telegram and AP wire
accounts.gist: The committee seized the officers as soon as the justice remanded the prisoners, hanged Sullivan and Howard, then broke into the jail for Payne; the work was 'thoroughly orderly' and approved by 'all classes'.

accounts.label: Seattle Post-Intelligencer (quoted in Honolulu)
accounts.gist: About 2,000 people, nearly all approving, watched; the officers were overpowered; it was 'the work of no mob' but of an outraged community.

accounts.label: San Francisco Chronicle narrative
accounts.gist: A fire-bell signal called the committee; about 500 battered in the jail doors, and Payne told a crowd of 800 or 1,000 that they would hang an innocent man.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Death by hanging at hands unknown; 'speedy and substantial justice has been subserved'.

accounts.label: Judge's address, April term
accounts.gist: The courts' record on homicide was strong, and a 'sense of duty' did not make the killing of Howard, Sullivan and Payne lawful.

framing.detail: The Sacramento Record-Union headlined 'Judge Lynch. Speedy Justice Meted Out' and closed with 'Everybody satisfied'.
The Post-Intelligencer denied it was a mob, and the Portland Oregonian, as quoted, said good men would 'say well done to the Committee of Safety'.
The Vancouver Independent called it a 'neck-tie party' and blamed slow courts; the Astorian cited the coroner's verdict as the town's feeling.
The Sag Harbor Express, reprinted in New Haven as 'Swift Vengeance', wished Guiteau had been 'served the same way'.
Eastern and Midwestern papers ran the wire under 'Murderers Lynched' or 'Lynch Law', some placing Seattle in Wyoming Territory.
The Walla Walla Statesman asked its citizens not to allow a lynching like Seattle's, and an April judge's address rejected the 'sense of duty' defense.

conflicts.note: The coroner's verdict is dated Jan. 18 and the special telegram describing the hanging is datelined Jan. 18, which favors the 17th/18th version; the '19th' in the Honolulu text may be an editor's gloss.
The Chronicle says the examination began at 9 and lasted about three hours (A16), consistent with early afternoon.
The 400 figure in the wire may refer to the party that went to the jail.
The Wyoming placement is a wire error.
